scenario_stem:
Saffron Dune Spices is a private limited company in Country X that blends and packs saffron-based spice jars. It sells 42,000 jars a year at $6.50 each, generating $273,000 in revenue, and employs 18 workers. Domestic sales have slipped since two supermarkets launched own-brand blends at lower prices, cutting Saffron Dune's market share from 15% to 11%.

A distributor in neighbouring Country Y has offered to sell 60,000 jars a year at $5.20 per jar if Saffron Dune licences its brand to a local bottler, or enters a joint venture with a Country Y importer. Country Y charges a 12% import tariff on finished spice jars and customers there prefer milder flavours. Saffron Dune must decide whether to stay purely domestic, licence its brand or form the joint venture.

questions.question_text: Define 'licensing'.
questions.model_answer: An agreement where a business (the licensor) grants another business (the licensee) the right to produce or sell its product using its brand, patent or process, usually in exchange for a fee or royalty [2].

knowledge_max_2: one business grants another the right to use its brand/patent/process
in exchange for a fee or royalty

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Saffron Dune Spices of expanding into Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Entering Country Y gives Saffron Dune access to a much larger customer base [k], because the distributor could sell 60,000 jars a year at $5.20, worth about $312,000 in extra revenue [app]. Opportunity 2: Selling abroad reduces dependence on the domestic market [k], which matters because Saffron Dune's domestic market share has already slipped from 15% to 11% [app].

knowledge_max_2: access to a larger market / more customers abroad
spreads risk / reduces reliance on the domestic market
application_max_2: 60,000 jars a year at $5.20 / about $312,000 extra revenue
domestic share fell from 15% to 11% / revenue $273,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Saffron Dune Spices could face if it expands into Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Country Y shoppers prefer milder flavours [k], so the existing saffron blends may not appeal and recipes may need reformulating to win buyers [app], increasing costs and risking a launch that fails to cover the entry investment [an]. Problem 2: The 12% import tariff on finished spice jars [k] would add about $0.62 to each $5.20 jar [app], cutting margins or pushing prices up so local competitors stay cheaper [an].

knowledge_max_2: cultural differences / tastes differ between countries
tariffs raise the cost of selling abroad
application_max_2: Country Y prefers milder flavours / recipes need reformulating
12% import tariff on $5.20 jar / about $0.62 added per jar
analysis_max_2: higher costs / launch may fail to cover entry investment
margins squeezed or prices raised / lose competitiveness

questions.question_text: Do you think Saffron Dune Spices should enter Country Y through licensing or a joint venture? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Licensing its brand to a local bottler would let Saffron Dune sell in Country Y without paying the 12% import tariff, because the jars would be filled locally [k], and could generate 60,000 jars at $5.20, about $312,000 a year, with little capital at risk [app]. However, licensing gives limited control over quality and over the milder recipe adaptation [an]. A joint venture with the Country Y importer would share the risk and bring market knowledge for the milder-flavour demand [k], while giving closer oversight and shared decision-making over the 60,000-jar plan [app], yet it locks capital into a long-term partnership and exposes Saffron Dune to the partner's performance [an]. Overall, licensing is the better first step given the share slide to 11% at home, because it is quick and low-risk [eval]; if Country Y orders exceed 60,000 jars a year, converting to a joint venture would then protect the brand [eval].

knowledge_max_2: licensing = local firm produces/sells for a fee, low capital risk
joint venture = shared ownership/risk with local partner and shared knowledge
application_max_2: 60,000 jars at $5.20 / about $312,000 a year for licensing
12% import tariff avoided locally / milder flavours / share fell to 11%
analysis_max_2: licensing avoids tariff and keeps capital free but weakens quality control
joint venture shares risk and adds local knowledge but locks capital in
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two entry methods
conditions/sequence suggested (license first, convert to JV if successful)

scenario_stem:
Tandoori Flame is a private limited company that runs 6 fast-casual tandoori restaurants in Country X, two in the capital and four in regional towns. Each outlet averages $410,000 in annual revenue, so the chain generated about $2.46 million last year and employs 84 staff across the six sites. Growth has slowed across Country X and two rival chains have opened competing restaurants near its two best-performing locations.

A group of investors in Country Z has asked to open Tandoori Flame outlets there under an international franchise agreement costing an upfront $40,000 per outlet plus 6% of annual sales. A company-owned Country Z restaurant would cost about $320,000 to open, and local customers prefer milder spice levels and different side dishes. The board must choose between the franchise programme and opening its own outlet.

questions.question_text: Define 'international franchising'.
questions.model_answer: A business (the franchisor) allows entrepreneurs in a foreign country (franchisees) to trade there using its brand, format and support in return for upfront fees and ongoing royalties [2].

knowledge_max_2: franchisee in another country trades under the franchisor's brand/system
in return for upfront fees and ongoing royalty payments

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Tandoori Flame might use international franchising to expand into Country Z.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Franchising allows rapid expansion abroad without Tandoori Flame funding each outlet itself [k], avoiding the roughly $320,000 opening cost of its own Country Z restaurant [app]. Reason 2: Each franchisee pays an upfront $40,000 fee plus 6% of annual sales [k], giving Tandoori Flame a steady royalty income on top of the $2.46 million domestic revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: fast growth abroad with less capital investment
upfront fees and ongoing royalty income for the franchisor
application_max_2: avoids about $320,000 cost of own outlet
$40,000 upfront plus 6% of annual sales / on top of $2.46 million

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Tandoori Flame could face if it expands into Country Z.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Country Z customers prefer milder spice levels and different side dishes [k], so the menu must change from the format that works in Country X [app], risking weak sales and food waste if the adaptation is judged wrongly [an]. Problem 2: Operating in Country Z means unfamiliar local laws and regulations [k], such as different food hygiene and employment rules that franchisees must follow [app], adding compliance delays and unexpected costs against the $410,000 average outlet revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: cultural differences / tastes and preferences differ abroad
unfamiliar laws and regulations / compliance burden
application_max_2: milder spice levels and different side dishes
franchisees must follow local rules / $410,000 average outlet revenue
analysis_max_2: weak sales and food waste if menu is wrong
compliance delays and added costs squeeze margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Tandoori Flame should use international franchising or open its own outlet in Country Z? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: International franchising would deliver $40,000 per outlet upfront plus 6% of annual sales [k], giving Tandoori Flame fee income without paying the $320,000 needed for its own restaurant [app], which also spreads risk across local franchisees rather than one $320,000 bet [an]. A company-owned outlet would give full control over the milder menu adaptation, service and standards [k], but the $320,000 cost would concentrate all losses in Tandoori Flame in an unfamiliar country [app], and any mistake on compliance or sourcing would hit the chain directly [an]. Overall, franchising is the better route now, because local partners understand Country Z tastes and share the risk while regular royalties build on the $2.46 million domestic base [eval]; a company-owned outlet should only follow once outlet sales prove the brand travels well [eval].

knowledge_max_2: franchising = fees plus royalties, low capital commitment, shared risk
own outlet = full control over quality/service but full cost and risk
application_max_2: $40,000 upfront plus 6% royalties per franchised outlet
$320,000 to open own outlet / built on $2.46 million base
analysis_max_2: franchise spreads risk and earns ongoing royalty income
own outlet concentrates cost and loss risk on Tandoori Flame
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options
conditions for a later company-owned move (proven outlet demand)

scenario_stem:
Kestrel Cycles is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing steel-frame commuter bicycles. It produces 8,000 bicycles a year at $340 each, generating $2.72 million in revenue, and employs 46 workers across welding, assembly and finishing. Domestic cycling commuter numbers have fallen since the pandemic boom ended, reducing sales by 9% over the past 2 years.

Country W has 120,000 cycling commuters and its distributors want to stock Kestrel bicycles, but riders there prefer lighter aluminium frames over steel designs. Redesigning the range would cost $400,000 and add $55 to the unit cost, while a 14% import tariff applies to finished bicycles entering Country W. The board must choose between localising the product range and exporting the current model.

questions.question_text: Define 'localising products'.
questions.model_answer: Adapting a product, such as its design, features, ingredients or packaging, to suit the tastes, laws and conditions of a foreign market rather than selling an identical product everywhere [2].

knowledge_max_2: product adapted to suit local tastes/laws/conditions
rather than selling an identical product in every market

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Kestrel Cycles of entering Country W.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Country W has 120,000 cycling commuters [k], a much larger potential market than the shrinking domestic one [app]. Opportunity 2: Establishing itself abroad diversifies revenue away from Country X [k], where sales fell 9% over the past 2 years, helping secure demand and jobs for the 46 workers [app].

knowledge_max_2: larger market / more potential customers abroad
diversification / less reliance on domestic demand
application_max_2: 120,000 cycling commuters in Country W
domestic sales fell 9% over 2 years / 46 workers

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Country W riders prefer lighter aluminium frames [k], so current steel models are unlikely to sell and Kestrel would need a $400,000 redesign [app], delaying entry and adding $55 to every unit cost [an]. Problem 2: A 14% import tariff on finished bicycles [k] would add about $48 to each $340 bike [app], forcing higher prices that could make Kestrel uncompetitive against local Country W brands [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrel Cycles should localise its bicycles for Country W or export its current model? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Localising the range would match Country W riders' preference for lighter aluminium frames [k], making the bicycles far more attractive across a commuter population of 120,000 [app], and it avoids the commercial failure of shipping steel models that dealers expect to remain unsold [an]. Exporting the current steel range avoids the $400,000 redesign and $55 higher unit cost [k], but a 14% tariff lifts each $340 bike by about $48 [app], and steel frames clash with local tastes, so volumes may be too low to profit [an]. Overall, localisation is the stronger option because $400,000 is only about 15% of annual revenue and unlocks the much larger Country W market [eval], while simply exporting the current model risks unsold stock and tariff-inflated prices [eval].

scenario_stem:
Amber Brook Cheese is a private limited company in Country X producing artisan hard cheeses. It makes 24,000 wheels a year at $28 each, generating $672,000 in revenue, and employs 25 workers across the dairy, rind-washing and maturation cellar. Domestic sales have been flat for 3 years and milk costs have risen by 18% since the last harvest.

A supermarket chain in nearby Country V will stock 15,000 wheels a year at $24 per wheel if Amber Brook meets its food-safety certification requirements within 9 months. Exporting would expose the business to a 10% import duty, freight costs of $3 per wheel and unfamiliar labelling rules. The board must decide whether to start exporting to Country V or focus on the domestic market and existing delis.

questions.model_answer: Selling goods or services produced in one country to buyers located in another country [2].

knowledge_max_2: selling goods or services to buyers in another country

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Amber Brook Cheese of exporting to Country V.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Exporting brings a firm order for 15,000 wheels a year [k], roughly $360,000 in extra revenue on top of its flat $672,000 domestic sales [app]. Opportunity 2: Selling in a second country spreads risk [k], so a downturn in Country X would no longer leave the 25 workers wholly dependent on the home market [app].

knowledge_max_2: larger market / additional sales revenue abroad

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A 10% import duty plus $3 freight per wheel [k] would cut the $24 export price to an effective $18.60 [app], squeezing margins at exactly the time milk costs have risen 18% [an]. Problem 2: Country V requires its own food-safety certification and labelling rules [k], which take up to 9 months to complete [app], delaying the first export order and tying up cash in compliance before any revenue arrives [an].

However, the 10% duty ($2.40 per wheel) and $3 freight leave about $18.60 per wheel [k], far below the $28 domestic price [app], and milk costs up 18% could make each export wheel barely profitable [an]. Overall, exporting is still worth pursuing if certification is secured within 9 months, because the extra volume should absorb fixed costs and offset the 18% milk-cost rise [eval]; if freight or duty terms cannot be improved, Amber Brook should delay exports and fix domestic sales first [eval].

recommendation sensitive to duty/freight negotiations

scenario_stem:
Lumen Haircare is a private limited company in Country X selling premium shampoos and conditioners through 14 retail stores. Revenue last year was $884,000 from 13,000 customers spending an average of $68 a year. Repeat purchase rates are 45%, but a rival brand has launched a similar range priced 15% below Lumen's products and is advertising heavily on television and online.

The marketing manager must recommend a new marketing strategy. Option A is a national social media influencer campaign costing $60,000 to attract new customers across the country. Option B is a $25,000 customer loyalty programme offering points and discounts to existing buyers. Cash is limited, so both options must be judged on lifting sales and protecting margins this year.

questions.question_text: Define 'marketing strategy'.
questions.model_answer: A long-term plan for how a business will use the marketing mix to reach its chosen target market and achieve its marketing objectives, such as gaining share or loyalty [2].

knowledge_max_2: long-term plan for using the marketing mix
aims at a target market and marketing objectives

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Lumen Haircare needs a clear marketing strategy before choosing between the two options.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A marketing strategy sets out which customers and which mix to target [k], so the $60,000 campaign and the $25,000 loyalty scheme are aimed deliberately rather than wastefully [app]. Reason 2: A planned strategy links promotion to measurable sales objectives [k], letting the 14 retail stores track whether either option lifts revenue above $884,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: strategy identifies the target market and marketing mix
strategy sets measurable objectives and direction
application_max_2: the $60,000 campaign vs $25,000 loyalty scheme differ

questions.question_text: Explain two ways a well-chosen marketing strategy could help Lumen Haircare counter the rival's 15% lower prices.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: A loyalty programme rewarding repeat purchases [k] would raise the 45% repeat-purchase rate by giving existing customers a reason to stay despite the rival's discount [app], defending the base of 13,000 customers rather than rebuying lost ones at great cost [an]. Way 2: Consistent, high-quality premium marketing [k] could strengthen Lumen's brand image so shoppers feel its price is justified [app], reducing pressure to match the rival's 15% price cut across the 14 retail stores [an].

knowledge_max_2: loyalty/relationship marketing retains existing customers

application_max_2: 45% repeat-purchase rate / base of 13,000 customers

analysis_max_2: higher repeat rate defends revenue without matching price cuts
premium image supports price and protects margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Lumen Haircare should choose the influencer campaign or the loyalty programme? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The influencer campaign costing $60,000 [k] could reach a far wider audience than the 13,000 current customers [app], building awareness and winning new buyers away from the rival [an]. The loyalty programme costs less than half as much at $25,000 [k], and by lifting the 45% repeat-purchase rate it protects the customers who already spend about $68 a year [app], which is cheaper than replacing customers lost to the rival [an]. Overall, the loyalty programme is the better first move because its $25,000 cost is affordable given limited cash and it directly defends Lumen's most profitable relationships [eval]; the influencer campaign should follow once retention improves and awareness converts into loyal buyers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: influencer campaign builds awareness and reach at higher cost

loyalty defence is cheaper than replacing churned customers
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options
sensible sequencing suggested (loyalty first, campaign later)

scenario_stem:
The Paper Lantern Bookshop is a private limited company that runs 2 independent bookshops in Country X, selling 19,000 books a year at an average price of $17. Revenue last year was $323,000 and the business employs 9 staff across the two shops. Online rivals have cut footfall by 22% over 3 years, and customers often enquire about events and recommendations before buying.

The owners must decide whether to employ a part-time marketing assistant for $14,000 a year to identify customer needs and build customer relationships, or keep spending unchanged. Option A grows the customer base through author events, reading groups and local promotion. Option B protects cash while the bookshop's remaining debts of $26,500 are repaid over the next 12 months.

questions.model_answer: Identifying and satisfying customer needs and wants [1]; maintaining customer loyalty and building customer relationships [1].

knowledge_max_2: identifying and satisfying customer needs and wants

questions.question_text: Explain two ways a marketing assistant could help The Paper Lantern Bookshop identify and satisfy customer needs.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: The assistant could run simple questionnaires and chat with shoppers about the books they want [k], turning direct feedback from the 19,000-book customer base into better stock decisions [app]. Way 2: The assistant could organise events such as author signings and reading groups [k], satisfying the enquiries about events and recommendations that online rivals ignore [app].

knowledge_max_2: market research (e.g. questionnaires) identifies customer needs

application_max_2: feedback from the 19,000-book customer base

questions.question_text: Explain two consequences for The Paper Lantern Bookshop if it does not respond to changing customer needs.
questions.model_answer: Consequence 1: Footfall, already down 22% over 3 years [k], would keep falling as customers choose rivals that meet their needs better [app], pushing annual revenue below $323,000 [an]. Consequence 2: Without understanding customer needs [k], the bookshop may stock unwanted titles and miss requests for events and recommendations [app], wasting shelf space and cash while customers defect to online sellers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think The Paper Lantern Bookshop should employ a part-time marketing assistant? Justify your answer.

However, the bookshop still owes $26,500 and wages cannot be used to repay that debt [k], so the $14,000 adds a fixed cost before any extra sales arrive [app], and if sales do not respond the hire strains cash further [an]. Overall, hiring the assistant is justified because $14,000 is under 4.5% of the $323,000 revenue and directly reverses the 22% slide by rebuilding the relationships that keep bookshops alive [eval]; the owners should set a 6-month sales target and review it to protect cash [eval].

scenario_stem:
Summit Grill Co is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing charcoal barbecues. Last year it sold 9,500 units at $95 each, generating $902,500 in revenue, and employs 31 workers at its assembly plant and packaging line. Its advertisements claim the grills are smoke-free, yet consumers report significant smoke in independent tests, and the advertising regulator has warned that the claim is misleading, carrying a possible $50,000 fine if not removed.

The board must choose between two options: keep the slogan and contest the regulator, risking the fine and reputation damage, or withdraw the campaign and launch an honest low-smoke advertisement costing $12,000 to reprint adverts and redesign packaging. The marketing manager believes honest promotion would build customer trust and loyalty over time.

Reason 2: Legal controls protect consumers from being deceived [k], so complying preserves the public trust on which $902,500 of annual barbecue sales depend [app].

scenario_stem:

Domestic growth has slowed and the owners have identified Country V, with 400,000 potential buyers, as a promising overseas market.

They must recommend a marketing strategy for Country V: either position the notebooks as a luxury niche product sold in 12 exclusive shops at $60 each, or sell them through supermarkets and department stores at $32 each for the mass market. Problem 2: Choosing the wrong positioning [k], for example pushing a $60 luxury notebook through supermarkets to mass-market shoppers not seeking hand-bound quality [app], would waste the marketing budget and blur the premium image built through the 5 premium stationery shops [an].

scenario_stem:

Last year it sold 250,000 meals at $5.40 each, generating $1.35 million in revenue, and employs 27 workers at its kitchen and cold-chain dispatch. The business wants to enter Country U, a neighbouring market three times the size of Country X, through an import distributor it has already signed.

The marketing manager must devise the marketing mix for Country U: either a premium range at $6.80 per meal targeted at affluent urban households, with gift-style packaging in specialist shops, or a family value range at $4.40 per meal aimed at price-sensitive shoppers in large supermarket chains. The distributor favours the family value option for the launch.

scenario_stem:
Ironwood Smokehouse is a private limited company in Country X producing smoked sausages and cured meats sold through 11 delicatessens. Revenue last year was $420,000 from 168,000 packs sold at $2.50 each, and the business employs 14 workers across smoking, curing and packing. A food importer in Country S has shown strong interest in stocking Ironwood products in delicatessens and gourmet shops across that country.

The importer offers to buy 20,000 packs a year at $2.20 each, but exporting would cost $90,000 to set up and require local labelling in the partner's language. The owners are unsure whether this beats spending $30,000 on a domestic loyalty scheme and tasting evenings to deepen relationships with delicatessen partners and shoppers across the region.
